issues.issue: The facility-of-payment provision begins mid-sentence ("...for the use of any beneficiary thereof who is a minor at the time of such payment"), the subject and the payments it applies to having dropped out of the text. A court would have to reconstruct what payments the Trustee may discharge in this manner.

The spendthrift protection is qualified at the outset by "To the extent that such power may be lawfully limited by this instrument", leaving the reach of the restraint to be settled by outside law rather than the text. A court would have to determine how far beneficial interests are in fact insulated from creditors and anticipation.

The incorporation of statutory trust powers excludes "Subparagraphs 1 through _ inclusive" with the closing figure illegible or blank, so the scope of the powers actually granted cannot be determined from the instrument. A court would have to decide which statutory powers the Trustee holds.

The successor trustee article stops mid-sentence at "then the", naming no successor and no appointment mechanism. A court would have to fill the gap and decide who may serve if the named bank resigns or is disqualified.

The Tennessee governing-law clause cannot be squared with the New York choice-of-law clause in the Metropolitan absolute assignment (c038), which Article II (c009) incorporates into this Trust Agreement verbatim. A court would have to decide which law governs the assignment of the Metropolitan certificate.

The exculpation, though badly garbled, excepts the Trustee's "own bad faith or negligence", which cannot be squared with Article V (c018) declaring that the Trustee "shall incur no liability" for purchases from or loans to the Grantor's estate. A court would have to decide which liability standard governs those transactions.

The Grantor's relinquishment of "all right to alter, amend, revoke [or] terminate" sits against Article I.B (c006), in which the Grantor expressly reserves the right to add property to the trust from time to time, and against the interlineated notation on the face of Article VI.A (c019). A court would have to decide how far the irrevocability clause forecloses post-execution changes to the instrument.

The absolute assignment reaches insurance "provided now or at any time hereafter" and under any group policy "hereafter issued in substitution", a scope wider than the two enumerated certificates that Article I.B (c004) makes the trust's "Policies of Insurance". A court would have to decide whether coverage substituted for the Metropolitan certificate is held on the trust's terms.

Effectiveness is made conditional on execution of the Waivers and Consents "set forth below", but that block (c040) is itself incomplete on the face of the document, leaving the condition's satisfaction unverifiable. A court would have to decide whether the assignment ever became binding on Metropolitan and, if so, that it relates back to the assignor's signature date.

The disclaimer of responsibility for "the validity, effect and sufficiency of this assignment for any purpose whatsoever" is unbounded and duplicates the assignee's own release (c042), leaving unclear whether the insurer disclaims even the effect of its own consent given in the Waivers and Consents (c040). A court would have to fix the scope of the disclaimer.

The sentence is mutilated — it joins "Metropolitan shall not be responsible for the trustee's application" to "full discharge of Metropolitan's liability" with the intervening words (the trustee's receipt operating as a discharge) missing from the page. A court would have to reconstruct what discharges Metropolitan on payment to the Trustee.

This New York choice-of-law clause conflicts with Article XI of the Trust Agreement (c030), which fixes Tennessee as the situs and Tennessee law as governing "in all respects", the assignment having been incorporated into the trust by Article II (c009). A court would have to decide which state's law construes the assignment.

The designation is rendered "revocuby dosignates", so it cannot be told whether the Trustee designated itself beneficiary revocably or irrevocably, and the class of beneficiaries designated is garbled. A court would have to construe who was designated and whether the designation could later be changed.

The Waivers and Consents sentence is missing its operative verb — the Group Policyholder and Metropolitan "hereby [waive] with respect to each above-stated Group Policy and Certificate, any provision therein against assignment" — so what was waived is not stated. Because c035 makes the assignment binding only if these waivers are executed, a court would have to determine the content and fact of the waiver.

The assignee accepts that the companies "will not otherwise communicate to me with respect to my rights under the policies, including amendments thereto", which sits against the later undertaking (c047) that billings "and any other written communications" will be mailed to the assignee's stated address. A court would have to decide what notice, if any, the Trustee-assignee was entitled to receive.

The release runs to "any responsibility for the sufficiency, validity, or effect of such assignment for any purpose", wording broad enough on its face to cover the companies' own failure to give the communications promised in the same instrument (c041, c047). A court would have to fix the outer boundary of "any responsibility ... for any purpose".

The lapse is triggered by failure to make contributory payments "as now or may be required in the future by Eastman", an obligation whose content Eastman alone may define at any time. A court would have to decide what the assignee was required to pay and when coverage lapsed.

Eastman's statement that it "will look to no one else other than me" — the Trustee-assignee — for contributory premiums cannot be squared with Article III of the Trust Agreement (c011), under which the Trustee "may, but shall not be obliged, to pay premiums" and bears no liability if they go unpaid. A court would have to decide whether the Trustee undertook a premium obligation the trust instrument disclaims.

The consent to schedules and methods "that may in the sole discretion of Eastman be changed from time to time" is open-ended and displaces the specific quarterly-in-advance, 30-day terms described in the next sentence (c046). A court would have to decide what billing terms actually bound the assignee at any given time.

The description of "Eastman's present payment schedules and methods of billing" is expressly provisional and is subject to unilateral change under c045, so it creates no fixed billing obligation. A court would have to decide whether the assignee could rely on quarterly advance billing with 30 days to pay.

The undertaking to mail billings "and any other written communications" to the bank's Kingsport address sits against c041, in which the assignee accepts that the companies will not otherwise communicate with it about its rights. A court would have to decide whether notice of lapse or amendment had to be mailed to the Trustee.

The reservation of Eastman's and Metropolitan's "right to amend or terminate any of the Policies" cannot be squared with the absolute assignment (c034) transferring to the Trustee all "incidents of ownership" and with Article II of the trust (c007) vesting the Trustee with the rights of absolute owner. A court would have to decide whose act controls when the group coverage is amended or ended.
